title: Uses of Aldehydes and Ketones: From Formalin to Vanilla
subject: Chemistry
objective: Where aldehydes and ketones turn up in daily life: formalin and Bakelite from formaldehyde, acetic acid from acetaldehyde, acetone as a solvent, and vanillin, cinnamaldehyde and benzaldehyde as smells and flavours, each explained from its C=O group.

fill.q: Formalin is an aqueous solution of about 40% ____.
Phenol and formaldehyde give the polymer ____.
The flavouring compound of vanilla is ____.

tf.q: Acetone is used as an industrial solvent.
tf.explain: Acetone and ethyl methyl ketone are common solvents.

tf.q: Formaldehyde is less reactive than acetone towards nucleophiles.
tf.explain: HCHO has no alkyl groups, so it is the most reactive.

tf.q: Benzaldehyde is used in perfumery and dyes.

ar.a: Acetone mixes with water and also dissolves grease.
ar.r: It has a polar C=O group and non-polar CH₃ groups.
Formaldehyde joins protein chains through –CH₂– bridges.

mcq.q: The compound used to preserve biological specimens is:
In the first step of Bakelite formation, the HCHO carbon is attacked by:
options: the ring carbon ortho to O⁻
mcq.explain: The ring's C=C π electrons at the ortho carbon attack.

num.q: How many alkyl groups are attached to the carbonyl carbon of formaldehyde?
steps: HCHO: two H atoms, no alkyl group

short.q: Explain, with curved arrows, the first step of the reaction of phenoxide with formaldehyde.
short.solution: The O⁻ lone pair moves into the ring; the ring C=C at the ortho carbon attacks the HCHO carbon; the C=O π pair moves onto O. After proton transfer the ring carries –CH₂OH.

match.explain: Each compound matches its main use.
